newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Probe accuses former Sri Lanka ministers of graft.
newsitem.headline: Probe accuses former Sri Lanka ministers of graft.

text.p: A Sri Lanka commission probing deals by the previous United National Party (UNP) government has found former ministers and officials guilty of misuse of power and recommended suspension of their civic rights.

Government officials said on Monday the Special Presidential Commission of Inquiry found ex-ministers Wijaypala Mendis and K.D.M. Chandra Bandra misused their positions to influence decisions that cost the exchequer millions of rupees.

The commission also found R. Paskaralingam, former secretary to the Treasury, and Ackiel Mohammed, then secretary to the power ministry and chairman of a privatisation sub-committee, guilty of using their positions to influence decisions in privatisation of a key state firm and a tender for bus chassis and bodies involving an Indian firm.
Paskarlingam left the country after the People's Alliance won parliamentary elections in 1994. Mendis and Mohammed were were not immediately available for comment.

The commission's report now goes to parliament for a vote. If it is approved, the accused will be stripped of their civic rights, depriving them of the right to vote and stand for public office. The attorney general's office can also take criminal action against the accused if it feels there is reason to do so.

The commission said in its interim report published over the weekend that Bandara, who is deceased, and Mohammed were found guilty of influencing the Divestiture Committee, which was repsonsible for the privatisation of a plant run by a unit of the state-owned Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC).
The commission said the Nylon 6 plant was sold for 227.7 million rupees, one-fifth of its valued price of 1.2 billion rupees, to South Korea's Tongyng Nylon Company Ltd in early 1990s.
It said the CPC had recommeded that only 60 percent of the shares be sold but Bandara got the committee sell 90 percent at a fraction of the valued price, losing the government millions of rupees.
Two other junior officials were not charged since they were forced to fall in line with the minister's decision, the commission said.

The commission said Mendis used his position to exchange 76 acres of his own land in northern Anuradhapura district with a similar acreage of coconut plantation belonging to the Livestock Development Board (LDB) in Dankutowa, just outside capital Colombo.
It said the exchange led to a commercial loss for the LDB as the market value of the coconut plantation was two million rupees ($34,662) and that of Mendis' farm 988,500 rupees.

The commission said it found Paskaralingam guilty of influencing a contract to buy 1,500 bus chassis and body kits from India's Ashok Leyland Ltd costing 43.7 million rupees ($757,365) in early 1990s.
It said Paskaralingam pushed the letter of intent for the contract to be issued to Ashok Leyland without cabinet approval.
Investigations into several other allegations against Paskaralingam, including those into other contracts for the local assembly of buses, were continuing, the commission said.
